focus: Exodus 22 continues the judgments of the Book of the Covenant with laws of restitution for theft, damage, and property held in trust, then laws that guard sexual responsibility and Israel’s exclusive worship of the LORD. The chapter turns to God’s protection of strangers, widows, orphans, and the poor, whose cry He promises to hear, and ends by calling Israel to live as a people holy to Him.

sections.title: Restitution for Theft and Damage
sections.summary: A thief must restore five oxen for an ox and four sheep for a sheep, or double if the stolen animal is found alive, and the law distinguishes a thief struck at night from one struck after sunrise. A man whose animal grazes in another’s field or whose fire spreads to another’s grain must make restitution.

sections.title: Goods Held in Trust and Borrowed
sections.summary: When goods or animals left in a neighbor’s keeping are stolen or lost, the judges decide disputed cases, and in some cases “an oath of the LORD shall be between them both” (Exodus 22:11). Responsibility depends on what happened, whether the owner was present, and whether the animal was borrowed or hired.

sections.title: Sexual Responsibility and Faithfulness to the LORD
sections.summary: A man who seduces an unbetrothed virgin must pay the bride-price and marry her, or pay it if her father refuses. Sorcery, lying with an animal, and sacrificing to any god “except to the LORD only” (Exodus 22:20) are capital offenses.

sections.title: The LORD Hears the Stranger, Widow, Orphan, and Poor
sections.summary: Israel must not oppress the stranger, for they were strangers in Egypt, and must not afflict the widow or fatherless, for the LORD will hear their cry. They must not charge interest to the poor and must return a pledged garment by sunset, for “when he cries to Me, I will hear, for I am gracious” (Exodus 22:27).

sections.title: A People Holy to the LORD
sections.summary: Israel must not revile God or curse a ruler, must not delay to offer the first of its produce, and must give its firstborn sons and animals to the LORD. “And you shall be holy men to Me” (Exodus 22:31), so they must not eat meat torn by beasts.

1.brief: A thief who steals an ox or sheep and slaughters or sells it must restore five oxen for an ox and four sheep for a sheep. Restitution is larger than the loss, making theft costly.
1.explain:
“If a man steals an ox or a sheep, and slaughters it or sells it,”

A thief who takes an animal and then “slaughters it or sells it” has disposed of it and cannot simply return it.

“he shall restore five oxen for an ox and four sheep for a sheep.”

He must repay several times over. Restitution is larger than the loss, making theft costly. The higher rate for an ox may reflect its value as a working animal.

2.brief: If a thief is caught breaking in at night and is struck so that he dies, there is no guilt for his blood. A householder defending his home in the dark is not held guilty.
2.explain:
“If the thief is found breaking in, and he is struck so that he dies,”

A thief caught “breaking in” is struck and killed by the householder.

“there shall be no guilt for his bloodshed.”

The householder is not guilty. The next verse shows this applies at night, when he cannot see who has broken in or what the intruder intends. A householder defending his home in the dark is not held guilty.

3.brief: If the sun has risen, there is guilt for his blood, and the thief must make full restitution or be sold if he has nothing. In daylight the householder must not kill, and the thief must still repay.
3.explain:
“If the sun has risen on him, there shall be guilt for his bloodshed.”

If it happens in daylight, the householder is guilty. In the light he can see the thief, call for help, or identify him later. Killing him then goes beyond self-defense.

“He should make full restitution; if he has nothing, then he shall be sold for his theft.”

The thief must still “make full restitution.” If he has nothing, he is “sold” into service to repay the debt. Theft must be repaid, even by labor.

4.brief: If the stolen animal is found alive in the thief’s possession, whether ox, donkey, or sheep, he must restore double. The restitution is twice what was taken.
4.explain:
“If the theft is certainly found alive in his hand, whether it is an ox or donkey or sheep, he shall restore double.”

If the stolen animal is still “alive in his hand,” the thief returns it and pays as much again. The restitution is twice what was taken.

5.brief: If a man lets his animal graze in another’s field or vineyard, he must make restitution from the best of his own field and vineyard. Damage to a neighbor’s crops must be repaid with the best one has.
5.explain:
“If a man causes a field or vineyard to be grazed, and lets loose his animal, and it feeds in another man’s field,”

A man lets his animal wander into a neighbor’s field or vineyard to graze.

“he shall make restitution from the best of his own field and the best of his own vineyard.”

He must repay “from the best” of his own crops. Damage to a neighbor’s crops must be repaid with the best one has.

6.brief: If a fire spreads through thorns and burns a neighbor’s grain or field, the one who kindled it must make restitution. Carelessness that harms a neighbor carries responsibility.
6.explain:
“If fire breaks out and catches in thorns, so that stacked grain, standing grain, or the field is consumed,”

A fire set to burn thorns spreads to a neighbor’s grain, whether stacked or still growing.

“he who kindled the fire shall surely make restitution.”

The one who started the fire is responsible. Carelessness that harms a neighbor carries responsibility, even when there was no intent to harm.

7.brief: If goods left with a neighbor for safekeeping are stolen and the thief is found, the thief pays double. The keeper is cleared when the real thief is caught.
7.explain:
“If a man delivers to his neighbor money or articles to keep, and it is stolen out of the man’s house,”

A man leaves money or goods with a neighbor for safekeeping, and they are stolen from the neighbor’s house.

“if the thief is found, he shall pay double.”

If the thief is caught, the thief pays “double.” The keeper is cleared when the real thief is caught.

8.brief: If the thief is not found, the keeper is brought before the judges to determine whether he took his neighbor’s goods. Suspicion is settled by a hearing rather than by assumption.
8.explain:
“If the thief is not found, then the master of the house shall be brought to the judges”

If no thief is found, the keeper himself is brought “to the judges.”

“to see whether he has put his hand into his neighbor’s goods.”

The judges determine whether he stole the goods himself. Suspicion is settled by a hearing rather than by assumption.
8.notes: The Hebrew word translated “judges” here is again elohim, which may mean God (see the note at 21:6). Either way, the case is brought before God’s appointed process of judgment.

9.brief: In any dispute over a lost or stolen item, both parties come before the judges, and the one they condemn pays double. Disputes over property are settled by fair judgment.
9.explain:
“For any kind of trespass, whether it concerns an ox, a donkey, a sheep, or clothing, or for any kind of lost thing which another claims to be his,”

The principle covers every kind of disputed property, animals, clothing, or any lost item.

“the cause of both parties shall come before the judges; and whomever the judges condemn shall pay double to his neighbor.”

Both sides present their case, and the one found guilty pays “double.” A false accuser and a thief face the same penalty. Disputes over property are settled by fair judgment.

10.brief: If an animal left in a neighbor’s keeping dies, is hurt, or is driven away with no one seeing, a further rule applies. The law addresses losses with no witnesses.
10.explain:
“If a man delivers to his neighbor a donkey, an ox, a sheep, or any animal to keep, and it dies, is hurt, or driven away, no one seeing it,”

An animal left in a neighbor’s care dies, is injured, or is taken, and “no one” saw what happened. There is no evidence either way.

11.brief: An oath of the LORD settles the matter between them, and the owner accepts it without requiring payment. In disputed cases without evidence, an oath before the LORD decides.
11.explain:
“then an oath of the LORD shall be between them both, that he has not put his hand into his neighbor’s goods;”

The keeper takes “an oath of the LORD” that he did not take the animal. The oath places the matter before God, who knows the truth.

“and the owner of it shall accept that, and he shall not make it good.”

The owner must accept the oath, and the keeper does not pay. In disputed cases without evidence, an oath before the LORD decides. A loss does not by itself prove guilt.
11.notes: Hebrews 6:16 notes that among people an oath for confirmation is the end of all dispute.

12.brief: If the animal was actually stolen from the keeper, he must make restitution to the owner. A keeper is responsible for guarding what is entrusted to him.
12.explain:
“But if, in fact, it is stolen from him, he shall make restitution to the owner of it.”

If the animal was “stolen” from the keeper, he must repay. A keeper is responsible for guarding what is entrusted to him, and theft suggests he was not careful enough.

13.brief: If a wild beast tore the animal, the keeper brings the remains as evidence and does not have to pay. Loss beyond the keeper’s control does not make him guilty.
13.explain:
“If it is torn to pieces by a beast, then he shall bring it as evidence, and he shall not make good what was torn.”

If a wild animal killed it, the keeper brings the remains “as evidence” and owes nothing. Loss beyond the keeper’s control does not make him guilty.
13.notes: Jacob told Laban that he had not brought him the animals torn by beasts but had borne the loss himself (Genesis 31:39). The law God later gave Israel set a different rule: the keeper could bring the remains as evidence and owe nothing. Amos 3:12 uses the picture of a shepherd rescuing two legs or a piece of an ear from a lion.

14.brief: If a man borrows an animal and it is injured or dies while the owner is absent, he must surely make it good. The borrower bears responsibility for what he borrows.
14.explain:
“And if a man borrows anything from his neighbor, and it becomes injured or dies, the owner of it not being with it,”

A borrowed animal is injured or dies while the owner is away.

“he shall surely make it good.”

The borrower bears responsibility for what he borrows.

15.brief: If the owner was present, the borrower does not pay, and if it was hired, the hire covers the loss. Responsibility depends on who was present and what was agreed.
15.explain:
“If its owner was with it, he shall not make it good;”

If the owner was present, the borrower does not pay. The owner could have protected his own animal.

“if it was hired, it came for its hire.”

If the animal was rented, the rental fee covered the risk. Responsibility depends on who was present and what was agreed.

16.brief: If a man seduces an unbetrothed virgin and lies with her, he must pay the bride-price and marry her. The law holds him responsible for the woman he has wronged.
16.explain:
“If a man entices a virgin who is not betrothed, and lies with her,”

A man seduces “a virgin who is not betrothed” and sleeps with her. The word translated “entices” means to persuade or seduce.

“he shall surely pay the bride-price for her to be his wife.”

He must pay “the bride-price” and marry her. The law holds him responsible for the woman he has wronged.
16.notes: The bride-price was a payment from the groom to the bride’s family. Deuteronomy 22:28–29 deals with a related but different case, in which a man seizes a virgin who is not betrothed and they are found out. There the law sets a payment of fifty shekels of silver and forbids the man ever to divorce her. Those terms belong to that case. This verse requires the bride-price, and 22:17 preserves the father’s right to refuse the marriage.

17.brief: If her father utterly refuses to give her to him, he must still pay money equal to the bride-price of virgins. The father may refuse the marriage, but the man still bears the cost of his act.
17.explain:
“If her father utterly refuses to give her to him,”

The father has the right to refuse the marriage.

“he shall pay money according to the bride-price of virgins.”

Even if there is no marriage, the man must still pay the full “bride-price of virgins.” The father may refuse the marriage, but the man still bears the cost of his act.

18.brief: “You shall not permit a sorceress to live.” Sorcery is treated as a capital crime against Israel’s covenant with the LORD.
18.explain:
“You shall not permit a sorceress to live.”

Sorcery was a capital crime in Israel. It sought power and knowledge from spirits rather than from God (Deuteronomy 18:10–12). It was a crime against Israel’s covenant with the LORD. These penalties belong to Israel’s covenant order as a nation under God. No believer or church carries them out (John 18:36; 2 Corinthians 10:4). The principle of capital punishment itself runs through Scripture (Genesis 9:6; Romans 13:4), and a government may justly apply it to serious crime with safeguards against error such as the requirement of two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 17:6).

19.brief: Whoever lies with an animal shall surely be put to death. This perversion is also a capital offense in Israel’s covenant order.
19.explain:
“Whoever lies with an animal shall surely be put to death.”

Bestiality was also a capital crime (Leviticus 18:23; 20:15–16). It violated the order God created and the purity He required of His people. This perversion is a capital offense in Israel’s covenant order.

20.brief: Whoever sacrifices to any god “except to the LORD only” shall be utterly destroyed. Worship of other gods strikes at the heart of Israel’s covenant with the LORD.
20.explain:
“He who sacrifices to any god, except to the LORD only, he shall be utterly destroyed.”

Sacrificing to another god breaks the first commandment (20:3). The phrase “utterly destroyed” means devoted to destruction, given over completely to God’s judgment. Worship of other gods strikes at the heart of Israel’s covenant with the LORD.
20.notes: The Hebrew verb is related to the word cherem, meaning something devoted to God, usually for destruction. It is used later of the cities of Canaan under God’s judgment (Deuteronomy 7:2; Joshua 6:17).

21.brief: Israel must not mistreat or oppress a stranger, “for you were strangers in the land of Egypt.” Israel’s own memory of oppression should make them kind to outsiders.
21.explain:
“You shall neither mistreat a stranger nor oppress him,”

A “stranger” was a foreigner living among Israel without land or family support. Israel must not “mistreat” or “oppress” him.

“for you were strangers in the land of Egypt.”

God gives the reason in Israel’s own history. Israel knew what it was to be outsiders under oppression. Their own memory of suffering should make them kind to outsiders.
21.notes: The command returns again and again (23:9; Leviticus 19:33–34; Deuteronomy 10:18–19). Leviticus 19:34 says, “you shall love him as yourself; for you were strangers in the land of Egypt.”

22.brief: Israel must not afflict any widow or fatherless child. The LORD places the most vulnerable under His special protection.
22.explain:
“You shall not afflict any widow or fatherless child.”

Widows and the “fatherless” had no husband or father to protect them in a society built around family. Israel must not take advantage of them. The LORD places the most vulnerable under His special protection.

23.brief: If they afflict them and they cry to God, “I will surely hear their cry.” God personally hears and defends the helpless.
23.explain:
“If you afflict them in any way, and they cry at all to Me,”

If anyone wrongs them and they cry out to God, God takes notice.

“I will surely hear their cry;”

God commits Himself to listen. God heard Israel’s cry in Egypt (3:7). He will hear the cry of the helpless in Israel too. God personally hears and defends the helpless.
23.notes: Psalm 68:5 calls God a father of the fatherless and “a defender of widows.”

24.brief: God’s wrath will burn, He will kill the oppressors with the sword, and their own wives will become widows and their children fatherless. Those who harm the vulnerable will suffer the same loss they inflicted.
24.explain:
“and My wrath will become hot, and I will kill you with the sword;”

God’s “wrath” will burn against the oppressor. He will act in judgment.

“your wives shall be widows, and your children fatherless.”

The punishment fits the crime. Those who harm widows and orphans will leave behind widows and orphans of their own. Those who harm the vulnerable will suffer the same loss they inflicted.

25.brief: If they lend money to a poor person among God’s people, they must not act like a moneylender or charge interest. Lending to the poor is to be an act of help, not profit.
25.explain:
“If you lend money to any of My people who are poor among you,”

God calls the poor “My people.” A loan to a poor Israelite is a loan to one of God’s own.

“you shall not be like a moneylender to him; you shall not charge him interest.”

Israel must not act “like a moneylender” or “charge him interest.” A loan to someone in need is to be an act of help, not a way to profit from his hardship.
25.notes: Leviticus 25:35–37 and Deuteronomy 23:19–20 repeat this law. Deuteronomy permits charging interest to a foreigner, which suggests the law concerns charity loans to fellow Israelites in need rather than business lending.

26.brief: If they take a neighbor’s garment as a pledge, they must return it before sunset. The law protects the poor from losing what they need to survive.
26.explain:
“If you ever take your neighbor’s garment as a pledge,”

A lender might take a borrower’s cloak as security for a loan.

“you shall return it to him before the sun goes down.”

The cloak must be back with its owner by nightfall. The law protects the poor from losing what they need to survive.

27.brief: The garment is his only covering to sleep in, and when he cries to God, “I will hear, for I am gracious.” God’s own gracious character stands behind the protection of the poor.
27.explain:
“For that is his only covering, it is his garment for his skin. What will he sleep in?”

The outer cloak was also a poor man’s blanket. God asks, “What will he sleep in?” He sees the cold night the poor man will face.

“And it will be that when he cries to Me, I will hear, for I am gracious.”

God ties the law to His own character. “I am gracious.” God’s own gracious character stands behind the protection of the poor. Mercy is to shape how His people use power and property.
27.notes: Deuteronomy 24:10–13 adds that the lender must not enter the borrower’s house to take the pledge, and that returning it will be counted as righteousness before the LORD.

28.brief: Israel must not revile God nor curse a ruler of the people. Respect for God and for those in authority belong together.
28.explain:
“You shall not revile God, nor curse a ruler of your people.”

Israel must not “revile God,” speaking of Him with contempt. Nor may they “curse a ruler,” one God has placed in authority. Respect for God and for those in authority belong together.
28.notes: Paul quoted this verse when he realized he had spoken harshly to the high priest: “You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people” (Acts 23:5).

29.brief: Israel must not delay offering the first of its produce, and “The firstborn of your sons you shall give to Me.” The firstborn sons belong to God and are given to Him by redemption, as Exodus 13:13, 15 directs.
29.explain:
“You shall not delay to offer the first of your ripe produce and your juices.”

Israel must not hold back “the first” of the harvest, the first grain and the first of the wine and oil. The first belongs to God and acknowledges that the whole harvest comes from Him.

“The firstborn of your sons you shall give to Me.”

The firstborn sons belong to God. They are given to Him by redemption, as 13:13, 15 directs, never by sacrifice.
29.notes: Proverbs 3:9 says, “Honor the LORD with your possessions,” giving Him the firstfruits of all your increase.

30.brief: The firstborn of oxen and sheep stay with the mother seven days and are given to God on the eighth day. God’s claim on the firstborn extends to the animals, with care for the young.
30.explain:
“Likewise you shall do with your oxen and your sheep.”

The same claim covers the firstborn of the animals.

“It shall be with its mother seven days; on the eighth day you shall give it to Me.”

The young animal stays with its mother for “seven days” before being offered on “the eighth day.” God’s claim on the firstborn extends to the animals, with care for the young.
30.notes: Leviticus 22:27 gives the same rule for all sacrificial animals.

31.brief: “And you shall be holy men to Me,” so they must not eat meat torn by beasts but throw it to the dogs. Israel’s holiness reaches even into what they eat.
31.explain:
“And you shall be holy men to Me:”

God calls Israel to be “holy” to Him, set apart in every part of life.

“you shall not eat meat torn by beasts in the field; you shall throw it to the dogs.”

Meat from an animal killed by wild beasts was unclean (Leviticus 17:15), probably because its blood had not been drained. It was to be given “to the dogs.” Israel’s holiness reaches even into what they eat.
